clue.text: Everything is this, as kith and kin can prove.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: completing the saying that everything is ..., judged only by comparison
second meaning: a member of one's family; the clue gives the plural group of which this is one

explanation.walkthrough: The first half fills the blank in the catchphrase 'everything is ___'; the second says family members are what this word names.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means judged by comparison, as in the saying; the noun means a family member, someone among your kin.

clue.text: Carry on! Sure, Em! Crazy! Show this to the boss!

indicators.note: crazy letters are wild and disordered, so these get rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone urges Em to keep going with a mad scheme, then show it to the boss.
explanation.walkthrough: The last sentence points to the same letters read as résumé, the CV you show an employer.
explanation.definitionFit: To resume is to continue after a pause, to carry on with what was stopped.

clue.text: Reluctant to a portion–it's revolting!

parts.note: loath means unwilling or reluctant
some is an amount or part of something

explanation.surface: Someone hesitant about a helping finds the food disgusting.
explanation.definitionFit: Loathsome describes something disgusting that causes hatred, a synonym of revolting in its sense of repellent.

clue.text: Sounds like this'll be Ian's symbol! Ouch!

indicators.note: says the answer is heard in the spoken words that follow

parts.note: the contraction of this will, spoken aloud

explanation.surface: Someone predicts a symbol for a man named Ian and then gets hurt.
explanation.walkthrough: Ian is the Scottish form of John, standing for any Scot; the plant is Scotland's emblem and is prickly, hence Ouch.
explanation.definitionFit: The thistle is the national emblem of Scotland, and its spiny leaves prick anyone who grabs it.

clue.text: That sassy kid has nothing but six on top, but it's so shaky!

definitions.note: the definition describes the thing; the answer is the noun for it

indicators.note: in a down entry the six sits above the rest

parts.note: VI is the Roman numeral for six
a brat is a cheeky, badly behaved child
O looks like zero

explanation.surface: A cheeky child has no clothes but a six on his shirt and can't stop trembling.
explanation.definitionFit: Vibrato is a regular pulsating wobble in pitch in singing or playing, a deliberately shaky tone.

clue.text: A sign of fragility or a nickname as an associate of the humanitarian organization?

parts.note: a handle is slang for a name or nickname, as on CB radio
to be with someone is to be in their company, associated with them
CARE is a long-standing international relief and aid agency

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a fragile-goods label could double as a nickname for a charity volunteer.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs on into 30-across. CARE, the aid agency founded in 1945, is written in capitals, which hides it in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the warning stamped on parcels holding breakable goods, a printed sign that the contents are fragile.

clue.text: Polysaccharide that the little woman might find is gone? Pretty starchy!

parts.note: Amy March is one of the four sisters in Little Women
to lose something is to find that it is gone

explanation.surface: A chemistry note on a sugar, a wife who misses something, and a starchy aside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The little woman' looks like a dated term for a wife, but it is one of Alcott's Little Women. The closing 'Pretty starchy!' is a nod: this is a part of starch.
explanation.definitionFit: Amylose is a polysaccharide, a long unbranched chain of glucose units that makes up part of starch.

clue.text: Delve around right to the point of the slow, sad song.

indicators.note: the word for delve goes around the abbreviation for right

parts.note: to delve is to dig

indicators.note: the point of a word is its tip, its last letter

parts.note: the second 'the' in the clue, whose final letter is taken

explanation.surface: A singer gets straight to the heart of a mournful song.
explanation.definitionFit: A dirge is a lament for the dead, a slow mournful piece of music.

clue.text: Weight loss? Or the way one elucidates, sometimes longer than we'd like.

definitions.text: the way one elucidates, sometimes longer than we'd like
definitions.note: the answer is a verb, what one does when elucidating at length

parts.note: ex means former, so pounds that are ex have been lost
pounds are units of weight

explanation.surface: A dieter's question, then a dig at people who explain things for too long.
explanation.walkthrough: Lost weight is ex-pounds: pounds that are former.
explanation.definitionFit: To expound is to explain or set out in detail, often at greater length than listeners want.

clue.text: Tom, this makes it sound like an Englishman talking about love apples, but it's just a saying.

definitions.text: Tom, this makes it sound like an Englishman talking about love apples
definitions.meaning: love apples are tomatoes; Tom said before the answer sounds like an English tom-AH-toes, as an American hears the answer
the answer is plural sayings, words to live by

explanation.walkthrough: Spoken American-style, the answer sounds like mah-toes, so 'Tom' plus it gives the English pronunciation of tomatoes.
explanation.definitionFit: Mottos are short sayings adopted as rules of conduct or slogans, maxims to live by.

clue.text: I swam, leapfrogging to a religious man.

indicators.note: in leapfrog one player jumps over the others to the far end, so the opening I jumps over the rest to sit at the back

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A swimmer brags about hopping over others on the way to meet a holy man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I swam' looks like the start of a story, but it is the letters to move.
explanation.definitionFit: A swami is a Hindu religious teacher or ascetic, a title of respect for a holy man.

clue.text: A frightening sound by the old buggy could lead you to mine!

parts.note: boo is the noise made to startle someone
taken as written
a trap is a light two-wheeled horse-drawn carriage of earlier times

explanation.surface: A scream near an old carriage might send you off towards a mine shaft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mine' reads as a pit for digging, but it is the buried explosive.
explanation.definitionFit: A booby trap is a hidden device set to catch the unwary, and one may draw you onto a concealed explosive charge.

clue.text: I remember her show–about headgear–but it could make a Brahmin sage.

indicators.note: the show's name goes about, that is around, the headgear

parts.note: I Remember Mama was a hit play, film and 1950s TV series, so the her of the title is Mama
a hat is the everyday piece of headgear

explanation.surface: Someone recalls a woman's show about hats, then muses it could produce a Hindu holy man.
explanation.walkthrough: The title I Remember Mama is the key: the woman remembered is Mama.
explanation.definitionFit: Mahatma, meaning great soul, is an honorific given to a revered Hindu sage or teacher.

clue.text: God! Thunder leads to water in France–a pond he lived on!

definitions.note: the definition points to a person, the man who lived by a pond, rather than to the pond

parts.note: Thor is the Norse god of thunder
eau is French for water

explanation.surface: An outburst at a storm, then a picture of French water and a man living by a pond.
explanation.walkthrough: 'God!' reads as an oath, but it is the thunder god. The pond is Walden Pond in Massachusetts.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry David Thoreau lived for two years in a cabin beside Walden Pond and wrote Walden about it.

clue.text: In Bristol, Ed overslept but made it in Ohio and Spain. (You can swear by it!)

definitions.text: made it in Ohio and Spain. (You can swear by it!)

indicators.note: the answer sits in the run of letters across these three words

parts.note: the letters run from the end of Bristol through Ed into the start of overslept

explanation.surface: Ed slept late in Bristol yet still got to Ohio and Spain, and that's a promise.
explanation.walkthrough: Bristol, Ohio and Spain all suggest places to visit; only the city that two of them share is wanted. 'Holy Toledo!' is an American exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: Toledo is a city both in Ohio and in Spain, and Holy Toledo is a mild American oath.

clue.text: Done to a T, by the sound of it, and ran around a tee!

definitions.text: Done to a T, by the sound of it
definitions.note: T sounds like tea, and tea leaves left soaking in hot water are steeped

indicators.note: the word for ran goes around the golf peg

parts.note: to speed is to run fast, so ran gives the past tense
taken as written, the golf peg

explanation.surface: A golfer finishes a perfect job and runs a lap of the tee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Done to a T' means perfectly; heard as 'done to a tea' it means soaked like a tea bag.
explanation.definitionFit: Tea is steeped when left to infuse in hot water, so done to a tea is steeped.

clue.text: Write in–to the Soviet Union, to Louisiana–that they are almost surrounded by water!

definitions.text: they are almost surrounded by water
definitions.note: the definition is plural, but describes the single landform

parts.note: to pen is to write
taken as written
SU is the abbreviation for the Soviet Union
LA is the US postal code for Louisiana

explanation.surface: Someone writes in to the Soviet Union and Louisiana about lands nearly ringed by sea.
explanation.walkthrough: Peninsula is Latin for almost an island.
explanation.definitionFit: A peninsula is a piece of land jutting out into the sea, bordered by water on most sides.

clue.text: A little play on this is bad, and makes one quite nervous and flighty.

parts.note: a skit is a short comic sketch

indicators.note: a bad version of the word is a corrupted one, its letters disordered

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Performing in a poor short play leaves someone jumpy.
explanation.definitionFit: Skittish describes a horse or a person who is easily startled, restless and excitable.

clue.text: Mrs. Spock, née Caputo, shows how to disable someone in the Sicilian manner.

definitions.text: disable someone in the Sicilian manner

indicators.note: the words show the answer in their letters, running across them

parts.note: the letters run from the end of Spock through née into the start of Caputo

explanation.surface: A Mrs. Spock, born Caputo, demonstrates a Mafia method of crippling someone.
explanation.walkthrough: The invented Mrs. Spock is there only to supply letters: the answer runs from the last letter of Spock through 'née' into Caputo.
explanation.definitionFit: To kneecap is to shoot someone in the knee as punishment, a mob or paramilitary practice associated with Sicily's Mafia.

clue.text: If you can leer crookedly, it's less dirty!

indicators.note: crooked means twisted out of line, so these letters are bent into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A lecher's sly glance turns out to be not so filthy after all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Less dirty' seems to describe the leer, but it is the comparative of a word for spotless.
explanation.definitionFit: Cleaner is the comparative form of clean, describing something with less grime on it.

clue.text: It's over, right? Your head knows it's a treat!

parts.note: something past is over and done with

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: taken as written; its first letter is used

explanation.surface: Someone asks if a matter is finished, then says the brain knows it's a reward.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastry, a sweet baked item such as a tart or Danish, is a classic indulgence or treat.

clue.text: Five not paid up makes for swearing!

parts.note: V is the Roman numeral for five
money still owing has not been paid

explanation.surface: Someone who hasn't paid back five dollars provokes a stream of curses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swearing' suggests cursing, but here it is the swearing of oaths.
explanation.definitionFit: Vowing is solemnly promising, swearing an oath to do something.

clue.text: Six valid, if imperfect, seasons inspired him.

definitions.note: the definition is the man, him, whom the seasons inspired

parts.note: VI is the Roman numeral for six

indicators.note: the word is valid only if made imperfect, its letters rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Six seasons count as valid, if flawed, and they inspired some person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seasons' sounds like years or harvests, but the reference is to a famous set of violin concertos.
explanation.definitionFit: Antonio Vivaldi, the Venetian Baroque composer, wrote The Four Seasons, concertos depicting spring, summer, autumn and winter.

clue.text: If you are on it, you are not a Quaker–or a Shaker–and the awful wrath about Ma's mate makes it worse.

definitions.text: If you are on it, you are not a Quaker–or a Shaker
definitions.note: on the warpath means bent on a fight, which pacifist Quakers and Shakers never are

indicators.note: the rearranged word goes about the husband
an awful version of the word is a mangled one, its letters disordered

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange
Ma's mate is Pa, her husband

explanation.surface: Pacifist religious groups are contrasted with angry folk whose rage at Ma's husband grows.
explanation.walkthrough: Quakers and Shakers are pacifist Christian sects; 'Shaker' also teases at someone trembling.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on the warpath is idiom for being angry and ready for a fight, the opposite of pacifist.

clue.text: It's normal, of course–look, it comes from the land of 10, 12 and 26.

definitions.text: it comes from the land of 10, 12 and 26

parts.note: par is the normal score on a golf course
to see is to look

explanation.surface: Someone says it is all normal and points to a thing from some far-off land.
explanation.walkthrough: 10, 12 and 26 are SWAMI, MAHATMA and VERANDA, words from India.
explanation.definitionFit: A Parsee is a member of the Zoroastrian community of India, descended from Persian refugees.

clue.text: This with Charlie is about trips to unwind in the return road.

definitions.text: This with Charlie is about trips
definitions.note: the definition is trips, and the title Travels with Charley, Steinbeck's book about a road trip with his dog, completes it

indicators.note: the word for unwind goes inside the turned-round road
a return journey goes back the other way, so the abbreviation is read backwards

parts.note: St, for street, stands in for road
to ravel is to untangle or unwind, as well as to tangle

explanation.surface: A book with a companion named Charlie is about journeys, unwinding on the road home.
explanation.walkthrough: John Steinbeck's 1962 Travels with Charley follows his drive across America with his poodle; Charley is spelt Charlie here.
explanation.definitionFit: Travels are journeys or trips, and the plural noun is also the first word of Steinbeck's travel book.

clue.text: Give a leg up to an investor–it's all in play!

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word is written bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written, the word to turn upwards

explanation.surface: Someone urges help for a financier who has everything riding on a show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give a leg up' looks like an idiom for helping; it is the instruction to raise leg, so it reads backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: An angel is a backer who invests money in a theatrical production, a play.

clue.text: You'll find a silver and agate display on the porch!

indicators.note: the answer is to be found in the letters of the next words
the words display the answer, laid out across them

parts.note: the letters run from inside silver through and into the start of agate

explanation.surface: A collection of silver and agate is set out on someone's porch.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is spread over three words, starting near the end of silver.
explanation.definitionFit: A veranda is a roofed open gallery or porch along the outside of a house.

clue.text: You could say a snack eaten by the high-level commander is, but it would not be considered very specific.

definitions.text: You could say a snack eaten by the high-level commander is
definitions.meaning: first meaning, taken literally: a snack a general has eaten is inside the general

definitions.text: it would not be considered very specific
definitions.meaning: second meaning: broadly, without going into particulars

explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a joke: the high-level commander is a general, so his eaten snack is inside him.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means generally or as a rule, speaking broadly instead of about particular cases.

clue.text: As around a contrasting coordinating conjunction, it really comes up against it!

indicators.note: the two letters go around the conjunction

parts.note: taken as written
but is the conjunction that joins two clauses in contrast

explanation.surface: A grammar lesson in which a conjunction meets strong resistance.
explanation.walkthrough: The grammar talk is the wordplay; 'really' is only emphasis.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that abuts another thing touches or borders it, meeting it edge to edge.

clue.text: A famous climber, Madam Secretary has lost fifty!

indicators.note: losing the fifty takes it out of her name

parts.note: Hillary Clinton was US Secretary of State when this puzzle appeared in 2009
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A noted mountaineer and a Secretary of State who has shed fifty pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: Both Hillarys, Clinton and the mountaineer Sir Edmund, spell the name with two Ls; dropping one gives the grid's six letters, so the definition names the climber by sound rather than exact spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Edmund Hillary, the New Zealand mountaineer, made the first confirmed ascent of Everest with Tenzing Norgay in 1953.

clue.text: See 5
